summary: Adds a new opcode to the SSH terminal modes encoding for the widely used IUTF8 mode. It indicates that the terminal input and output use UTF-8 text.

eli5.summary: When you connect to another computer, this lets your terminal say that it is using the modern letters-from-every-language text format.

questions: what is ssh terminal mode opcode 42
subtitle: A new SSH terminal mode opcode that tells the server a terminal is using UTF-8.

tldr.problem: The SSH terminal modes encoding had no way to express IUTF8, a commonly used mode saying terminal input and output use UTF-8.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines opcode 42 for IUTF8, followed by one uint32 argument: 0 for disabled, 1 for enabled.
tldr.outcome: Clients can pass the UTF-8 setting to the server in a pty-req. The server can use it to decide how many bytes of input make one character during line editing.

sections.title: The Missing Terminal Mode
sections.content:
The SSH connection protocol (RFC 4254) encodes terminal modes for the pty-req channel request. A commonly used mode, IUTF8, tells the terminal driver to assume terminal I/O uses UTF-8.

It is typically used by the kernel's terminal driver on the server to decide how many bytes of input to treat as one logical character during line editing. SSH had no encoding for it until this document.
sections.eli5: Some letters take more than one byte. The server needs to know your terminal is using these, so it does not cut a letter in half when you press backspace.

sections.title: Opcode 42
sections.content:
The opcode value 42 is defined for IUTF8. As RFC 4254 specifies for opcodes 1 to 159, it is followed by a single uint32 argument. The value 0 means the mode is disabled and 1 means enabled.

As with every encoded terminal mode, the client SHOULD transmit a value if it knows about the mode, and the server MAY ignore it.
sections.eli5: Your computer sends a note numbered 42 with a yes or a no. The other computer may choose to ignore the note.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA added opcode 42, mnemonic IUTF8, to the Pseudo-Terminal Encoded Terminal Modes registry, described as terminal input and output being assumed to be encoded in UTF-8.

The security considerations of RFC 4254 apply, and the mode is believed to add no new implications. Because it goes with UTF-8, the UTF-8 considerations also apply: terminal drivers using the bit for UTF-8-aware line editing should consider how they treat illegal sequences, overlong encodings and redundant representations of composed characters.
sections.eli5: The new note adds no new danger, but a terminal that understands UTF-8 should be careful with broken or oddly written letters.

items.label: IUTF8
items.desc: Terminal input and output assumed to be UTF-8; followed by one uint32 argument.
